headline: TREK’s browser/MCP and sensitive-data handling create medium-to-high interaction risks; marker is isolated but can still be misused as an instruction source.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK uses browsers and MCP, so it can ingest external or shared content that may be treated as instructions. marker has no browser, MCP, filesystem write, or network egress, so it is not an active injector, but its document-processing outputs could still be copied into TREK. The pathway exists in common workflows, though not proven by direct interaction evidence.
conditions: IF TREK ingests marker-produced text through MCP, browser automation, or copy-paste without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF marker outputs are manually pasted into TREK as instructions, TREK may follow attacker-controlled content.
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction-following on imported text.
Add provenance labels to marker outputs before import.
Require a human review step for any browser-sourced content.
Restrict TREK MCP tools to allowlisted actions only.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: TREK touches highly sensitive data classes including API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and email addresses, and it has files plus allowlisted network egress. marker has no filesystem read/write or network egress, which lowers direct leakage risk, but if TREK forwards marker-processed documents or logs into its own backend, sensitive data can still be exposed. The pairwise pathway is plausible in default TREK workflows.
conditions: IF TREK processes documents containing secrets or personal data and sends them to external APIs, leakage can occur.
IF marker outputs are stored in TREK uploads or logs, those contents may be retained with sensitive travel data.
mitigations: Avoid placing secrets in TREK-managed documents.
Review TREK logs and uploads for sensitive content.
Turn off any optional external API calls for sensitive workflows.
Use separate accounts for sensitive and non-sensitive travel data.
requires-engineering: encrypt or redact sensitive fields before TREK persistence.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: marker cannot write files, modify git state, or use network, so it cannot directly contend for mutable resources. TREK supports real-time collaborative sessions and multiple instances, but the profile does not show unrestricted shared writes to the same directory or git state. The overlap is therefore limited and mostly avoids direct capability conflict.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable TREK workspace with write access added externally, conflicts may appear.
IF an operator manually copies marker output into TREK while TREK sessions are editing the same record, last-write-wins issues can occur.
mitigations: Keep marker read-only in the workflow.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same TREK record.
Use one TREK session per dataset during review.
Export marker output to a separate review file.
requires-engineering: add locking or optimistic concurrency checks for shared records.

D_cascading_error.rationale: marker produces document-processing output that TREK could plausibly ingest as travel-planning input. TREK’s collaborative, AI-built-in workflow suggests it may act on or render that input, so an error in marker can cascade into incorrect reservations, budgets, or plans. There is no evidence of verification between them, so the interaction is inferred and should be treated as a default-path risk.
conditions: IF TREK uses marker output as authoritative travel content without verification, downstream plans may be wrong.
IF marker misreads a document and TREK auto-populates reservations or budgets from it, the error propagates.
mitigations: Require human verification before TREK acts on imported text.
Compare marker output against the source document.
Flag low-confidence extractions for review.
Limit automation to non-destructive draft creation.
requires-engineering: add validation rules before TREK commits actions.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles sensitive personal and account data, including email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while marker is a document-processing tool with no stated residency or retention controls. Because the pair lacks documented compliance boundaries, the safest reading is a retention and handling mismatch risk rather than a proven residency violation. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from the pairwise flow.
conditions: IF marker-derived documents containing personal data are stored in TREK files or logs, retention obligations may apply.
IF TREK is used for regulated travel records without documented deletion/export handling, compliance gaps may arise.
mitigations: Do not store regulated data in TREK unless necessary.
Review TREK retention settings and log contents.
Separate personal and non-personal travel records.
Document deletion/export procedures before use.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based retention and subject-rights workflows.
